events.text:
🪖 Why the barefoot Houthis are a formidable force the world can no longer ignore
 
Ansar Allah has announced fresh attacks on Saudi oil facilities, its international airport, and pro-Saudi forces and command centers in Yemen, while continuing[ its siege of Taiz.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/77545)
 
The Houthis continue their operations despite pressure from Saudi-led coalition forces, raising questions about the sources of their resilience and staying power.
 
Partisans of God's legitimacy
 
The Ansar Allah movement emerged from Yemen’s Zaydi Shia community in Saada governorate. Its origins are commonly traced to the founding of the Believing Youth movement in 1992, led by Zaydi cleric Sayyid Hussein Badr al-Din al-Houthi. The title “Sayyid” denotes descent from the Prophet Muhammad. Zaydism holds that legitimate imams must descend from the Prophet through his daughter Fatima and Ali and meet specific religious and personal qualifications.
 
An estimated 35% to 45% of Yemen’s population is Zaydi. Furthermore, the Zaydi Imamate ruled northern Yemen for nearly a thousand years before being overthrown in 1962. This makes the Houthis presently led by Sayyid Abdul-Malik al-Houthi not simply a militant group, as some Western media portray them, but a movement with religious legitimacy in the eyes of its supporters.
 
Beyond its religious foundations, the movement’s core ideology centers on national liberation from US, Israeli, and Saudi domination.
 
Al-Houthi vs. Ali Saleh
 
Hussein al-Houthi's confrontation with Ali Abdullah Saleh's government escalated in the early 2000s over Saleh's close ties with the US and Saudi Arabia, particularly his support for Washington's "war on terror." In June 2004, government forces launched a campaign to arrest al-Houthi, triggering the first Saada war. They killed him in September 2004 after months of fighting.
 
That didn't stop the movement. Saleh’s forces fought five more bloody wars against the Houthis from 2005 to 2010, only to see the movement grow from 200 to between 2,000 and 10,000 fighters. In 2014, the Houthis seized the Yemeni capital of Sanaa. By 2024, they had reportedly recruited 350,000 fighters.
 
Houthi military arsenals
 
Over the years, Ansar Allah has not only amassed substantial military stockpiles but also developed domestic production of drones and missiles between 2018 and 2025, according to research by the US-based Century Foundation (TCF). Since 2015, the Houthis have deployed ballistic and cruise missiles, rockets, air-defense systems, aerial and maritime drones to strike targets up to 2,600 km from their territory, as well as a [vast variety of explosives.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75587)
 
Since 2015, a single demining group has cleared 460,000 landmines, IEDs and unexploded ordnance belonging to the group across Yemen, while maritime forces have intercepted up to 50,000 weapons and over 2 million rounds of ammunition bound for the Houthis. These figures are believed to represent only a fraction of the group’s arsenal.
 
The group maintains a sophisticated network of [supply channels spanning the Middle East, Africa, Asia and Europe. ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75872)This suggests it is not solely dependent on Iran for weapons and supplies but has developed its own procurement networks and regional ambitions.

All flights grounded following US Air Route Traffic Control Centers communications issues 
💬 “There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted. Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis,” the Federal Aviation Administration announced on X. 
Over 3,300 flights have been canceled and approximately 10,000 delayed, with disruptions expected to continue into the weekend.
This is the second time all US Air Route Traffic Control Centers, responsible for guiding aircraft, have been grounded since 9/11.
